name: WeatherPro: Forecast & Radar (ex-MeteoGroup, now DTN)
price: Originally ~€2.99/$2.99 one-time paid app; now free download with Premium subscription required for core features (maps layers, long-range forecast, ad-free)
complaints: Bought the app outright, then MeteoGroup/DTN moved key features behind an additional Premium subscription — 'paid for the app but still can't see cloud layers without paying again'
Long-time loyal users (10+ year Europeans, it was THE premium Euro weather app) leaving angry reviews saying they feel milked; 'useless and waste of money', 'support is useless'
DTN also killed sibling app MeteoEarth, feeding abandonment distrust
Cluttered redesign; paying subscribers say the interface got worse while the price structure got more aggressive
freeIncumbentRisk: High-ish: Google feed weather, Weawow, and free national-met-service apps cover casual use. But WeatherPro's payers are weather enthusiasts who already proved willingness to pay for premium Euro model data. A fair one-time-price, no-sub, data-rich weather app for that cohort is exactly the gap.
moatNotes: Real moat problem is forecast-data licensing cost (why every incumbent went subscription). Cloneable if built on free/cheap sources (Open-Meteo, MET Norway, NWS) with premium UX; the 3.49-star incumbent proves 91k raters care enough to be angry rather than silently leave.

name: Storm Shield (E.W. Scripps / WDT severe-weather alerts)
price: Historically paid (~$2.99) + alert add-ons; now subscription — users report $1.49/mo silently raised to $5.99/mo
complaints: Subscription price raised from $1.49/mo to $5.99/mo with no warning
Support email listed on the store bounces — 'address doesn't exist' — classic corporate abandonment (Scripps media conglomerate side project)
App failed to deliver alerts during actual tornado warnings — the one job it exists for
Android version rated 3.0 while iOS sits at 4.76: Android build is the neglected one
freeIncumbentRisk: Medium: WEA government alerts, FEMA app, and local-TV-station apps are free, but they are county-based/noisy. Storm Shield's pitch (polygon/storm-based, voice-read alerts for exact GPS location) is a genuine paid JTBD — people pay for life-safety reliability. NWS polygon data is free to consume.
moatNotes: Underlying NWS CAP/polygon data is free; the product is reliable push infrastructure + battery-safe location. Small feature surface, safety-critical reliability is the whole product — an actively maintained clone with working alerts wins on trust alone. Push-delivery SLA is the hard part.

name: ShopSavvy - Barcode & QR Scanner (price comparison)
price: Free download, paid-gated: ShopSavvy Pro subscription (~$4.99/mo, lifetime option) to remove ads / unlock price-history features
complaints: 30-second ad after every scan — users say Googling the UPC by hand is now faster than the app's core function
Users who paid the Pro subscription to disable ads report ads still showing across Search/Saved/More tabs, with support not responding
Price data wrong or missing best offers (showed $9.45 'best price' when Walmart had $4.48)
Reviews explicitly blame ownership change / recent updates for the downfall of 'what early on seemed a really useful app'; frequent crash-to-home when tapping items
freeIncumbentRisk: High: Google Lens, the Amazon/Walmart apps, and OS-level scanners do free scan-to-search. Clone viability rests on one-scan multi-retailer price comparison + price-history alerts, which the free incumbents deliberately silo. Ad-free one-time-purchase positioning directly attacks the resentment.
moatNotes: Barcode scanning is commodity (ML Kit); the moat/cost is retailer price-data aggregation (scraping/affiliate feeds). 17M installs with a sub-4.1 rating and paying-but-still-ad-served users is a large aggrieved base, but data ops make this the heaviest lift of the three.
